blocks.p: The next step is differentiating between coping with defense and anchoring in your Polyvagal safety state. These are different, and accurately understanding the two will help you identify if you are experiencing actual safety state activation or managing defensive state activation. I'll use the example of a panic attack to illustrate the difference.

When we cope, we tolerate a panic attack and attempt to get through it by reducing its intensity until it subsides. With coping, we don't truly anchor in our Polyvagal safety state. Examples of coping could be distracting yourself with TV or mindlessly snacking on something. I think of "coping" as dealing with or managing. The goal of coping is to reduce your negative experiences of dysregulation.

There is absolutely nothing wrong with coping, by the way. If you need to get through dysregulation through distraction, that's fine. You can learn from it and set yourself up with more safety for the next time.

Safety anchoring is different. Anchoring means accessing your body's state of safety. It's more than coping. It's mindfully attuning to the cues and experience of safety. Safety anchoring when feeling the onset of a panic attack might include:

ul: going for a mindful walk and noticing your surroundings.
feeling your muscles moving as you release your mild panic energy through movement.
using your senses to connect to the present moment.

blocks.p: Safety anchoring isn't easy. But practice helps: a lot. These ideas above might not immediately be usable for you right now, but as you practice safety, they may become so. You need to do these three things before you can realistically anchor yourself in safety:

ol: Experience your safety state, maybe for the first time
Figure out what brings you to your safety state again
Practice accessing your safety state regularly.

blocks.p: As you practice accessing your safety state, you build up your potential to be able to do so again and again. And yes, this includes even moments of escalating anxiety and even panic. As you strengthen your safety state, defensive activation becomes more tolerable. Likewise, as defensive activation becomes more tolerable, you will have more capacity to feel dysregulation with compassion.

Your safety state is not always on, nor is it always off. And it's never fully active, nor is it ever fully inactive. We talk about the autonomic states in fairly one-dimensional terms for ease of discussion. But really, the safety state's activation level exists on a spectrum. We need to stop viewing safety as all-or-nothing. Instead, let's look at it as a range of potential.
I'll identify four major points on the Safety Spectrum and invite you to identify where you may exist. I will also explore strategies one typically uses and what may be more helpful.

The Spectrum's first point is minimal safety state activation. Due to minimal safety comes increased defensive activation, likely autonomic dysregulation. Autonomic dysregulation occurs when defense is active without a strong safety activation. Autonomic dysregulation leads to emotional and cognitive dysregulation. The individual on this side of the spectrum experiences intense emotions like panic, rage, overwhelm, and dissociation.

Emotional and autonomic dysregulation lead to relationship and behavioral struggles. This individual will have significant difficulties maintaining relationships or starting new ones. They may even have a hard time recognizing safety in others. And if they do, they have a hard time trusting it and being vulnerable with healthy boundaries. This individual self-soothes their dysregulation through mindless behavioral adaptations like self-harm, drug use, bullying/abuse, disordered eating, sexual preoccupation, or isolation. They may also regularly check out by endlessly scrolling through social media and binging on a streaming service.

This person maybe knows they need help, but often they don't. If they know they need help, they put it off. Or they think nothing will help them and it's pointless to try. They end each day regretting not having done anything differently, actively shaming themself and reinforcing their dysregulation. They live with regret and guilt, which only fuels their behavioral adaptations.

We know this individual has minimal safety state activation because they cannot exist in the present moment without self-soothing. They are not interested in their inner world. They don't have self-compassion. They don't have healthy relationships. They are incapable of much connection with others, themselves, or the present moment. At least, not consistent or significant amounts of these things.

This person struggles with their inner world. They are almost unable to identify their emotions, sensations, and impulses. They are familiar with their cognitions, as they spend a lot of time in their heads dishing out guilt, regret, blame, and shame. But they are largely disconnected from their other SSIEC domains.

If this describes you, don't think it's hopeless! After all, you're reading this. You want change. You can be in stillness, read, think, learn, reflect, and maybe even take the next step. Your situation is not hopeless.

If this describes you, perhaps the best thing you can do is to start setting up [passive environmental safety](piece:anchor-environment). I also encourage you to seek out professional help. Use this as an adjunct to therapy or other professional services, not a standalone intervention.

If this doesn't describe you, there's a good chance you've lived this type of existence. There may have been a period of your life (or two or three…) where you had minimal safety state activation. You may be emerging from this and working your way into mild safety state activation.

The second point on the Spectrum is mild safety state activation. Mild safety activation brings moments of positive experiences. But there is also significant worry, anxiety, irritation, anger, sadness, and other defensive emotions.

This individual has some safety in their system. They want to make changes in life but struggle. They may even be putting "the work" into going to therapy, taking courses, telling their trauma narrative, and learning from social media psychology influencers.

They have relationships personally and professionally, but they are not fulfilling. They want to connect with others but struggle. Dysregulation pops up frequently, but this individual can mostly deal with or cope with it. They know they must be more proactive in making changes but lack consistency. They try something out, then lose interest or lose dedication. They latch onto self-help topics that make sense but don't consistently put them into practice.

This person does well with passive safety cues or co-regulation from another. They use safety cues, knowing what helps them calm down their dysregulation. But it's hit and miss, and nothing seems to solve the problem entirely, leading to frustration with trying to change.

They're familiar with their defensive states: their history, emotions, and thoughts. But they struggle with identifying underlying sensations and impulses. They have some fluency in identifying and talking about their emotions, especially the ones from defensive states. But they lack the ability to truly experience their inner world with compassion.

This person might even excel at talking around their experiences, but never quite touching upon their inner pains with compassion. Instead of feeling safe and connected to themselves and their inner pains, they focus on their shadow, ego, parts, diagnoses and other labels, astrological signs… well, you get the idea. They spend time around their pains and get closer to safety and connection, but mostly in a cognitive way, pursuing answers and insight endlessly.

If this describes you, congrats, you're on the right track! Much of this tells me you are actively putting things into practice and want to change your life. But it's difficult. No, not because something is wrong with you. It's because your safety state needs strengthening. As your safety state becomes stronger, the practices you implement will be much more effective.
At this point on the Spectrum, you should lay a solid foundation of passive safety cues and experiment with active safety cues. You're not yet anchoring into safety, but you're on your way!

Coping is very appropriate for this point on the Spectrum. You would do well with actively preparing for dysregulation by creating a "regulation station." Basically, get together what you know works and have it ready to go when needed. You may do better with sensory safety cues, which trigger safety using your five senses.

The third point on the Spectrum is moderate safety state activation. When moderately activated, the individual will have consistent experiences of connection with themself, with safe others, and with their environment. This individual can experience the full range of their emotions without getting easily sucked into dysregulation.

Moderate safety state activation allows the individual to feel their defensive activation. They won't dismiss, minimize, reduce, or try to numb it away. They will recognize when they are feeling defensive activation and allow it. Defensive emotions won't derail their plans for the day or their ability to function in relationships. They will recognize defensive activation as normal based on context and listen to their emotions with interest.

This individual can offer co-regulation from their moderate activation. They function well as a parent, employee, and partner. They have healthy boundaries overall and don't sacrifice their values for the selfish benefit of another. Instead, they are willing to compromise to ensure their and others' needs are met.
They can also access their mixed states of play, stillness, and intimacy. Safety is strong enough to intermingle with the defensive states and regulate them for pro-social purposes.

The person at point 3 on the Spectrum has gone beyond cueing and can anchor into safety. This person is settling into their safety state, experiencing the underlying sensations and impulses of connection. They can accept passive safety cues and purposefully experience safety anchors. Clients and [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) students report much more distress tolerance as they achieve a moderate level of safety state activation.

Point 3 is imperative for recovering from trauma. A moderate amount of safety activation seems to allow the natural process of self-regulation to unfold. In other words: Polyvagal ladder climbing. Moderate safety provides a nice grounding to begin to allow defensive state activation lightly. With moderate safety, someone in a shutdown may notice emerging sympathetic activation.

Point 3 is essential for building the vagal brake as well. Stuck defensive activation emerges as the vagal brake strengthens. If you can mindfully exist in safety and mindfully allow for defense, this opens the possibility of further ladder climbing and safety state strengthening. Part of this is purposefully shifting from safety to defense and back and forth. This pendulation process helps strengthen the safety state pathways.

If this describes where you're at on the Spectrum, keep doing whatever you do. You're on the right path. You may be ready to experience your defensive states and stuck trauma directly, without relying on psychobabble and woo-woo as cognitive crutches. Ensure you have passive safety cues in your home, solid relationships, healthy boundaries, self-compassion, and fulfilling hobbies and occupation. We don't need perfection in all these areas, but we strive for good enough, at least.

Also, focus on connecting with others. At this point, you have good connections with the right people and yourself. But make sure you express this to those who deserve to hear it. Sure, they may know it already. But take it beyond knowing and into experiencing. You may know you love yourself but express it deliberately. Your spouse may know you love them, but make sure you express it to them. Your friends, children, parents, and pets may all know, but take it to the next level.

The 4th point on the Safety Spectrum brings more obvious and robust experiences of positivity and connection. This individual is deeply anchored in their safety state. They are emotionally well-regulated and highly co-regulative.

Of course, this person can still access their defensive states when needed. When danger is present, they will still shift into sympathetic activity. They will accurately neurocept cues of danger and descend their Polyvagal ladder. When danger subsides, they climb back up their ladder and offer connections to others who may need it.

They won't become dysregulated with minor "danger" cues, like interpersonal issues. They retain their strong anchoring in safety. They keep their values while also offering safety cues to the other person. They can understand the viewpoint of another without feeling personally threatened. They can express empathy and understanding even when disagreeing on the most personal issues.

This individual understands the interconnectedness of everything in life. They feel awe, wonder, and appreciation for existence. They know they are a small but important facet of the universe. This individual instinctively strives to be a positive force but feels no compulsion to trample on others to make that happen. Instead, they are mindful of others and respect their rights. They also profoundly appreciate and expect the best out of them, while also being realistic about what others are capable of.

Connection is not scary in Point 4. It's invited with healthy boundaries and mutual respect. When others cannot do the same, the individual on Point 4 keeps the invitation for connection open. But they also create a healthy boundary until the other person can accept the invitation from their safety state.

If this describes you, keep doing what you're doing. Keep making connections and providing co-regulation. As you do, the people you connect with will become more likely to make new connections and offer co-regulation. In time, we may create a web of innumerable co-regulative connections. You are a small but significant part of that.

It's normal to fluctuate from one side of the Safety Spectrum to the other. Your Point on the Safety Spectrum is not static; it changes throughout the day, over the years, and in response to perceived danger. As your life context changes, your Point may change. As you recover from trauma, your Point will change.

The Points on the Safety Spectrum describe an entire person, but that's sort of misleading. In reality, you may fit onto Point 3 in one context, but Point 1 in another. Like when you're at work, you're firmly anchored in your safety state in Point 4. But, when you get home, you slide to Point 1.
To complicate things further, you may also have a Baseline of 3 across all of your life contexts. But every now and again, you shift to a 1 in a specific Moment.

"Moments" are experiences that come and go. They may be brief connections with another or extended periods of awe. They can be seconds (Deb Dana's "glimmers" and "glows") or extend for hours. Moments indicate temporarily sliding to the right on the Spectrum, increasing in safety activation compared to your Baseline. For example, spending time with friends may bring you to Point 3 for a Moment, whereas Point 2 is your Baseline.

"Baseline" refers to your more predictable safety state activation over a long time period, like days to decades. Your safety Baseline Point will slide to the right on the Spectrum as you develop the strength of your safety state (your vagal brake). For example, your Baseline may be a 1 when beginning therapy and slide to Point 3 eventually. Your Baseline may decrease with major life changes, like losing a loved one, moving homes, or changing careers.
Let's put the pieces together.

You currently have a certain Baseline Point on your Safety Spectrum. That Baseline can increase toward more and stronger safety state activation. It increases as you give yourself more Moments of safety, especially when combined, later, with mindfully experiencing your stuck defensive state(s).

To come out of your traumatized state, you need more than literal safe people and places. You need to mindfully experience your traumatized state and allow the natural process of self-regulation. Individuals with Safety Baselines closer to the left side of the Spectrum will have more self-regulation obstacles. At Baseline Point 1, your self-regulation capacity is minimal. But the good news is you can still have Moments of safety, probably passively at first. As you practice safety and increase your Baseline to 2 and further, your capacity for self-regulation and trauma recovery increases.

I laid out the Spectrum as I see it. There are, of course, even further extremes of the Spectrum. I use "Minimal" safety state activation on the far left, not "No" activation. And on the far right, I use "Strong" activation and not "Perfect and Constant" activation. I suppose the Spectrum can extend further in both directions, though I don't know how that would look, nor how realistic they are. I'm sure we could also divide up the Points into more Points, but I think the four suffice.

Recalling the development of the Polyvagal states within us may be helpful, from the first tiny mammals to humans. Mammals did not evolve to be in a constant state of ventral activation. Mammalian states fluctuated according to the demands of survival in the present moment. In danger, the sympathetic pathways allowed for evasion or aggression. Dorsal caused them to go limp and mimic a corpse when in a life-threat. Ventral allowed for homeostasis when safe and for co-regulation. It also allowed for a vagal brake, keeping the heart at a calmer pace, even if accurately neurocepting danger.

The ventral safety state can also combine with defensive states, repurposing them for prosocial and homeostatic functioning. Safety plus flight/fight is play with another; safety plus dorsal is stillness when alone or intimacy with a trusted other.

Our states work with each other, not against each other. In any specific moment, one state may be more influential than another, sure. However, I don't think one gets so dominant that it has all of the autonomic activation and the other two have none. Nor should that be the goal. All of the states serve a function at all moments of the day.

The Safety Spectrum should serve as a general concept to help you identify where you are on your overall progress. Like Deb Dana's Polyvagal Ladder metaphor, it's conceptual. Not literal. There is no easy, objective, and reliable way to measure what percentage of safety is active in your system, but it opens an avenue for self-reflection and a way to subjectively track your progress.

blocks.prompt: Where are you on the safety spectrum most days (your baseline)? When did you last have a moment further to the right?
